common_name: Double Standard Sweet Corn (Bicolor SE Hybrid Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced (SE) bicolor hybrid bred for tender, evenly sweet kernels and reliable germination in cooler soil than supersweet types allow.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows rather than one long row, since corn is wind-pollinated and needs neighbors on all sides for full ears. Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced bicolor hybrid that carries the classic tender-creamy texture of older SE types rather than the crisper, sometimes tough texture of supersweet (sh2) hybrids, and it germinates dependably in soil a bit cooler than most supersweets tolerate, which suits an early planting. Ears fill out with a mix of white and yellow kernels and hold good eating quality in the garden for several days past peak without turning starchy as fast as older open-pollinated types. Succession-sow every two to three weeks through early summer for a extended harvest, and pick when silks have browned and a punctured kernel weeps milky juice.

common_name: Cocke's Prolific Corn (Colonial Virginia Multi-Ear Dent Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60F; Cocke's Prolific is one of the oldest documented Virginia dent corns, grown since the colonial era for its habit of setting two to four ears per stalk rather than the single large ear typical of most modern corn.

directions: Direct sow in blocks for good wind pollination and give plants extra room, since Cocke's Prolific grows tall and leafy and puts its energy into multiple smaller ears rather than one big one. This Virginia heirloom dent corn has been passed down since the 1700s and was long valued by small farmers precisely because a prolific, multi-eared plant hedges against a poor pollination year better than a single-ear hybrid does. Ears are white to pale yellow dent kernels good for cornmeal and grits once fully dried on the stalk, and the tall, leafy plants also produce useful fodder. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it by distance or timing from other corn varieties to keep the seed line true for saving.
sources: Monticello Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

common_name: Tennessee Red Cob Corn (Appalachian Heirloom White Dent Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile soil; Tennessee Red Cob is an Appalachian heirloom dent corn grown for cornmeal and grits, easily identified in the field by its distinctive dark red cob under white kernels.

directions: Sow directly in well-drained soil in blocks for reliable pollination, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest since this is a grinding corn rather than a fresh-eating sweet corn. Tennessee Red Cob is a long-grown Appalachian and upland Southern heirloom prized by home millers for producing a notably white, fine-textured meal, with the vivid red cob making it easy to sort visually from other corn at harvest. Plants tolerate the hot, humid conditions and periodic dry spells typical of Southern summers reasonably well once established, and the variety has a long history of on-farm seed saving. Store dried ears in a mouse-proof container with good airflow, and shell only what you need for milling at a time to keep meal fresh.
sources: Sustain Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy Seed Program

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in acidic, well-drained, pine-bark-amended soil; Britewell is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release bred for consistently heavy yields and needs a second mid-season rabbiteye cultivar nearby for good cross-pollination.

directions: Plant dormant or container bushes in winter in raised, sulfur-acidified beds where native soil is not already acidic, and keep a permanent layer of pine bark mulch over the root zone. Britewell is a University of Georgia rabbiteye selection valued by growers for consistently heavy, reliable cropping of firm, medium-blue berries with good flavor on a moderately vigorous, upright-spreading bush, ripening in the mid-season window alongside cultivars like Tifblue. Plant with a second mid-season rabbiteye for cross-pollination and fuller berry set, and feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest. Renewal-prune the oldest wood out each winter to keep young, productive canes coming and sustain the heavy yields the variety is known for.
